b: Beth de Araújo delivers an unflinching exploration of childhood trauma, eliciting a miracle performance from the young Mason Reeves.

How do you take the most abhorrent act a human can commit and distil it into language simple enough for a child to understand? This is one of the questions posed by writer/director Beth de Araújo in Josephine, her second feature film, which premiered to raves at Sundance in early 2026. After getting separated from her father while out running, eight-year-old Josephine (Mason Reeves) watches a man brutally assault a female jogger in the woods. As Josephine is the sole witness, her testimony is crucial to the rapist’s conviction. But how can a child testify about something she cannot comprehend?

De Araújo wastes no time in getting to the point. The film is told through Josephine’s perspective, meaning that early into the first act we are forced to watch the assault take place with her. It’s an intense, violent sequence that leaves you gasping for air and a bold choice by de Araújo that will undoubtedly spark debate. In the aftermath of the crime, the film’s visual language unravels alongside the safety net of childhood. Dizzying angles, POV shots and an anxiety-inducing courtroom single take are all employed by cinematographer Greta Zozula to devastating impact. Miles Ross’ unrelenting score soundtracks this loss of innocence, veering into a dissonant, disturbing, electronic territory as the world around Josephine becomes increasingly hostile.

Unable to understand what she saw, Josephine begins to act out. She is constantly haunted by the spectre of the bad man, the storybook monster lurking in the woods who is suddenly made flesh. For all their efforts, her parents are ill-equipped to help Josephine make sense of the situation, their differing parenting styles shown to be a result of how they themselves were parented. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan are excellent as Josephine’s parents, Damien and Claire. Tatum is at the top of his game as a protective father, immediately kicking into action mode by enrolling Josephine in self-defence classes. Chan, although not given as much to work with, delivers a heartbreaking performance as a mother desperate to protect her child but also aware that, as a girl, the threat of assault is tragically part of life.

None of this would be as impactful without Reeves’ knockout performance, marking her feature film debut after de Araújo scouted her at a San Francisco farmer’s market. Her turn as a child robbed of innocence is breathtaking and masterful, demonstrating a wisdom far beyond her years. With Josephine, de Araújo examines a justice system so broken that even a child can see the cracks. Darkness aside – and there is plenty in this film – de Araújo finds hope and light in Josephine and her loving parents, who are just good people wanting to help deliver justice despite the immense personal cost.
